2. 
The Origins and History of the APA. The APA was enacted in 1946, 
after more than a decade and a half of “pitched political battle for the life of the 
New Deal.” George B. Shepherd, Fierce Compromise: The Administrative 
Procedure Act Emerges from New Deal Politics, 90 Nw. U. L. Re v . 1557, 1560 
(1996). Although the political fight that produced the APA was “perhaps more 
about the New Deal’s substance than it was about the comparatively dry 
mechanics of the administrative process,” the final compromise arrived in the 
form of a framework statute heavily informed by pre-APA statutes, case law, 
and administrative practice. Emily S. Bremer, The Rediscovered Stages of 
Agency Adjudication, 99 WASH. U. L. Re v . 377, 396 (2021). Especially 
influential was the work of the Attorney General’s Committee on 
Administrative Procedure, which was convened at the request of President 
Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1939 to provide a “scientific” study of the actual 
procedures and practices of existing administrative agencies. The Committee 
produced 27 monographs on individual agencies and regulatory programs. 
Based on this voluminous research, the Committee also prepared a 474-page 
report to Congress, which included competing legislative proposals from the 
liberal majority and conservative minority of the Committee. The Committee’s 
proposals were introduced in Congress and, following a delay caused by World 
War 11, the APA was enacted. The work of the Attorney General’s Committee 
was published by the Senate as part of the APA’s legislative history, and it 
supplied what Professor Kenneth Culp Davis described as an “intellectual 
foundation” for the statute. In 1947, the Department of Justice published the 
Attorney General’s Manual on the Administrative Procedure Act, which 
provided guidance to agencies about how to comply with the new law. The 
Manual can shed further light on the APA’s meaning and operation, as the 
excerpt below demonstrates.
